name: Retro interface
philosophy: Use recognizable interface materials as storytelling while retaining contemporary input, responsiveness and access. Nostalgia should lower the cost of understanding, not reproduce old limitations.
influences: Desktop window chrome, early web navigation, bitmap lettering and beveled controls. The selected era must be named; mixing every decade erases specificity.
characteristics: Window or panel metaphors with legible hierarchy
typography: Use a system font for body text and a licensed pixel face only at sizes it was designed to render. Test device pixel ratio; never rasterize all content to emulate an old display.
color: Define flat surfaces, highlights, shadows and selected states as roles. Avoid approximating a specific vendor's identity without purpose. Modern contrast requirements still apply.
spacing: Build a consistent inset/bevel system. Give controls contemporary hit areas even when their visible chrome is compact. Do not force a 640px desktop into a phone viewport.
composition: Window frames can group independent tasks, but unnecessary overlapping dialogs obstruct reading. Keep a clear main document with optional playful panels.
imagery: Use original diagrams or licensed period artifacts with attribution. Do not redistribute operating-system logos, sounds or icon packs on the assumption that old means public domain.
iconography: A small original pixel set may work. Essential actions need visible text and accessible names. Emoji are not a substitute for a coherent period icon set.
components: Beveled buttons must have distinct press and focus states. Tabs follow standard keyboard interaction. A decorative title bar should not misleadingly advertise dragging or resizing.
interaction: Support conventional browser links and back navigation. If dragging is implemented, also provide a non-drag alternative. Don't make a fake desktop the only route to essential content.
motion: Short stepped transitions may fit. Avoid flashing cursors, boot sequences that gate content, and compulsory sound. User-triggered audio needs a stop control.
mobile: Let windows become normal stacked panels. Keep close actions reachable and avoid accidental destructive dismissal. Decorative chrome can reduce while the era remains visible in type and materials.
accessibility: Use semantic controls beneath visual chrome; test zoom, keyboard order, contrast and touch. Any novelty control needs an understandable conventional fallback.
mistakes: Fake controls that imply behavior but do nothing
amateurish: A screenshot-like desktop with inaccessible text and nonfunctional window controls.
exceptional: A clear era, original assets and convincing tactile states coexist with effortless modern navigation.
implementation: Use CSS inset shadows and borders for bevels, not images of controls. Retain real buttons, headings and links. Collapse window columns below their content minimum.
libraries: Plain CSS and semantic HTML suffice. Use a maintained accessible behavior library if adding dialogs; its visual style can be replaced.
evaluation: Do all apparent controls perform the action they imply?
Can the whole experience be used without drag, sound or precise pointer input?
evidence: Original design recipe; source-linked engineering constraints. Not a validated causal model of visual quality.
